source_text: Aeque sono nominum duceris, cum uirtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae et regem Assyriorum sic accipis, quasi bellatorem portendant Christum creatoris, non animaduertens quid scriptura praemittat: quoniam priusquam cognoscat (puer) uocare patrem et matrem, accipiet uirtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae aduersus regem Assyriorum. ante est enim inspicias aetatis demonstrationem, an hominem iam Christum exhibere possit, nedum imperatorem. scilicet uagitu ad arma esset conuocaturus infans, et signa belli non tuba sed crepitacillo daturus, nec ex equo uel de curru uel de muro sed de nutricis aut gerulae suae collo siue dorso hostem destinaturus, atque ita Damascum et Samariam pro mammillis subacturus! aliud est, si penes Ponticos barbaricae gentis infantes in proelium erumpunt, credo, ad solem uncti prius, dehinc pannis armati et butyro stipendiati, qui ante norint lanceare quam lancinare. enimuero, si nusquam hoc natura concedit, ante militare quam uirum facere, ante uirtutem Damasci sumere quam patris et matris uocabulum nosse. sequitur, ut figurata pronuntiatio uideatur. sed et uirginem\'. inquit, \'parere natura non patitur, et tamen creditur prophetae\'. et merito. praestruxit enim fidem incredibili rei rationem edendo, quod in signum esset futura: propterea, inquit, dabit uobis dominus signo: ecce uirgo concipiet in utero et pariet filium. signum autem a deo, nisi nouitas aliqua monstruosa, iam signum non fuisset. denique Iudaei, si quando ad nos deiciendos mentiri audent, quasi non uirginem, sed iuuenculam concepturam et parituram scriptura contineat, hinc reuincuntur, quod nihil signi uideri possit res cotidiana, iuuenculae scilicet praegnatus et partus. in signum ergo disposita uirgo mater merito credetur, infans uero bellator non aeque; non enim et hic signi ratio uersatur. sed signo natiuitati nouae adscripto exinde post signum alibi ordo iam infantis edicitur, meI et butirum manducaturi, — nec hoc utique in signum: [est: malitiae non assentaturi] et hoc enim infantiae est — sed (et) accepturi uirtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae aduersus regem Assyriorum, serua modum aetatis et quaere sensum praedicationis, immo redde euangelio ueritatis quae posteriori detraxisti: et tam intellegitur prophetia quam renuntiatur expu-ncta. maneant enim orientales illi magi infantiam Christi recentem auro et ture munerantes: et accepit infans uirtutem Damasci sine proelio et armis. nam praeter quod omnibus notum est orientis uirtutem, id est uim et uires, auro et odoribus pollere solitam, certe est creatoris uirtutem ceterarum quoque gentium aurum constituere, sicut per Zachariam: et ludas praetendet apud Hierusalem et congregabit omnem ualentiam populorum per circuitum, aurum et argentum. de illo autem tunc auri munere etiam Dauid: et dabitur illi ex auro Arabiae, et rursus: reges Arabum et Saba munera offerent illi. nam et magos reges habuit fere oriens et Damascus Arabiae retro deputabatur, antequam transcripta esset in Syrophoenicen ex distinctione Syriarum, cuius tunc uirtutem Christus accepit accipiendo insignia eius, aurum scilicet et odores, spolia autem Samariae ipsos magos, qui cum illum cognouissent et muneribus honorassent et genu posito adorassent quasi deum et regem sub testimonio indicis et ducis stellae, spolia sunt facti Samariae, id est idolatriae, credentes uidelicet in Christum. idolatriam enim Samariae nomine notauit, ut ignominiosae ob idolatriam, qua desciuerat tunc a deo sub rege Hieroboam. nec hoc enim nouum est creatori, figurate uti translatione nominum ex comparatione criminum. nam et archontas Sodomorum appellat archontas Iudaeorum et populum ipsum populum Gomorrae uocat, et idem alibi: pater, inquit, tuus Amorreus et mater tua Cethea, ob consimilem impietatem, quos aliquando etiam suos filios dixerat: filios generaui et exaltaui. sic et Aegyptus nonnumquam totus orbis intellegitur apud illum superstitionis et maledictionis elogio. sic et Babylon etiam apud Iohannem nostrum Romanae urbis figura est, proinde magnae et regno superbae et sanctorum dei debellatricis. hoc itaque usu magos quoque Samaritarum appellatione titulauit, despoliatos quod habuerant cum Samaritis, ut diximus, idolatriam. aduersus regem autem Assyriorum aduersus Herodem intellege, cui utique aduersati sunt magi tunc non renuntiando de Christo, quem intercipere quaerebat.
pass_a_gloss: You are equally led by the sound of names, when you take the virtue of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria and the king of the Assyrians in such a way, as if they were bearing Christ the creator as a warrior, not noticing what the scripture says beforehand: that before the child knows how to call father and mother, he will take the virtue of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. For it is first necessary to examine the demonstration of age, whether he can already show Christ as a man, let alone as an emperor. Certainly, the infant would not be called to arms with a cry, and the signs of war would not be given with a rattle but with a trumpet, nor would he designate the enemy from the neck or back of his nurse or carrier, but from a horse or chariot or wall, and thus he would subdue Damascus and Samaria for his nurse's milk. It is different if, among the Pontic barbarian nations, infants rush into battle, I believe, anointed with oil first, then armed with swaddling clothes and paid with butter, who know how to wield a lance before they know how to tear. For if nature nowhere allows this, to wage war before becoming a man, to take the virtue of Damascus before knowing the name of father and mother. It follows that the prophetic statement seems figurative. But also, a virgin, he says, does not bear by nature, and yet it is believed by the prophet. And rightly so, for he has established faith by giving a reason for the incredible thing, which was to be a sign: therefore, he says, the Lord will give you a sign, behold, a virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a son. But a sign from God, unless it is some new and monstrous thing, would not be a sign. Finally, the Jews, if they ever dare to lie to us, as if the scripture did not contain that a virgin, but a young woman, would conceive and bear, are refuted by this, that nothing of a sign can be seen in a common thing, namely, a young woman's pregnancy and childbirth. Therefore, a virgin mother, disposed as a sign, is rightly believed, but an infant warrior is not equally so; for there is no reason of a sign here. But with the sign of a new birth written down, then after the sign, the order of the infant is already announced, namely, that he will eat butter and honey, and this is not certainly a sign, for it is also characteristic of infancy, but he will take the virtue of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Keep the measure of age and seek the sense of the prophecy, or rather, restore to the gospel of truth what you have taken away from the later one: and thus the prophecy is understood as it is announced and repeated. For the eastern magi, honoring Christ's recent infancy with gold and frankincense, remain; and the infant took the virtue of Damascus without battle and arms. For apart from what is known to all, that the virtue of the East, that is, the power and strength, is accustomed to be rich in gold and fragrances, it is certainly the creator's virtue to establish the gold of other nations as well, just as through Zechariah: and Judah will offer before Jerusalem and gather all the strength of the peoples around, gold and silver. And concerning that gift of gold, David also says: and it will be given to him from the gold of Arabia, and again: the kings of Arabia and Sheba will offer gifts to him. For the East and Damascus were almost considered part of Arabia before it was transferred to Syrophoenicia, distinguished from the Syrians, whose virtue Christ took by taking their insignia, namely gold and fragrances, but the spoils of Samaria are the magi themselves, who, having recognized him and honored him with gifts and worshiped him as God and king under the testimony of the star and its leader, have become the spoils of Samaria, that is, of idolatry, believing in Christ. For he has noted idolatry by the name of Samaria, as it is ignominious due to idolatry, by which it had departed from God under King Jeroboam. Nor is it new for the creator to use figurative language by translating names from a comparison of crimes. For he also calls the rulers of the Sodomites the rulers of the Jews and calls the people themselves the people of Gomorrah, and elsewhere: your father, he says, is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite, due to similar impiety, whom he had sometimes also called his own sons: I have begotten and exalted sons. And thus Egypt is sometimes understood as the whole world, in the context of superstition and curse. And thus Babylon is also a figure of the Roman city, accordingly great and proud in its kingdom and a persecutor of God's saints. Therefore, the magi are also titled by the name of Samarians, despoiled of what they had with the Samarians, as we said, idolatry. But against the king of the Assyrians, understand against Herod, whom the magi certainly opposed at that time by not renouncing Christ, whom he was seeking to intercept.

pass_b_english: You let the sound of names push you around just the same. You treat the virtue of Damascus, the spoils of Samaria, and the king of the Assyrians as if they marked Christ the Creator as a warrior, without noticing what Scripture says up front: before the child knows enough to call father and mother, he will take the virtue of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians (Isaiah 7:14). You have to check the age first, to see whether he can even present Christ as a man, let alone as an emperor. The infant is not going to be summoned to arms by a cry; the signals of war come from a trumpet, not a rattle; and he does not pick out the enemy from the neck or back of his nurse or carrier, but from a horse, a chariot, or a wall — and so he would subdue Damascus and Samaria for his milk. It would be different if, among the Pontic barbarians, infants charged into battle — anointed with oil first, then armed with swaddling bands and paid in butter — who know how to thrust a lance before they know how to tear meat. Since nature nowhere allows anyone to wage war before becoming a man, or to take the virtue of Damascus before knowing the words father and mother, the prophetic statement must be figurative. But a virgin, he says, does not give birth by nature, and yet the prophet is believed — and rightly so. He has grounded faith by supplying a reason for the incredible thing that was to be a sign: therefore, he says, the Lord will give you a sign: behold, a virgin will conceive in her womb and bear a son (Isaiah 7:14). A sign from God, unless it is some new and monstrous thing, would not be a sign at all. Finally, when the Jews dare to lie to us, claiming Scripture speaks of a young woman, not a virgin, conceiving and bearing, they are refuted by this: nothing of a sign can be seen in an ordinary thing, namely a young woman's pregnancy and childbirth. So a virgin mother, arranged as a sign, is rightly believed; an infant warrior is not equally so, for there is no sign-reason here. But with the sign of a new birth recorded, the infant's career is announced next: he will eat butter and honey — not as a sign, since that belongs to infancy anyway — but he will take the virtue of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Keep the measure of age and seek the sense of the prophecy; rather, restore to the gospel of truth what you stole from the later text, and the prophecy is understood exactly as it is announced and repeated (Isaiah 7:14). The eastern magi remain, honoring Christ's recent infancy with gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11); and the infant took the virtue of Damascus without battle or arms. For besides what everyone knows — that the virtue of the East, that is, its power and strength, is accustomed to abound in gold and fragrances — it is certainly the Creator's virtue to constitute the gold of other nations as well, just as through Zechariah: Judah will offer at Jerusalem and gather all the wealth of the surrounding peoples, gold and silver (Zechariah 14:14). And concerning that gift of gold, David says: it will be given to him from the gold of Arabia, and again: the kings of Arabia and Sheba will offer gifts to him (Psalm 72:15). The East and Damascus were practically reckoned as part of Arabia before it was transferred to Syrophoenicia, distinguished from the Syrians, whose virtue Christ took by taking their insignia, namely gold and fragrances. But the spoils of Samaria are the magi themselves, who, having recognized him and honored him with gifts and worshiped him as God and king under the testimony of the star and its leader, became the spoils of Samaria — that is, of idolatry — believing in Christ. He has branded idolatry with the name Samaria, because it was ignominious for idolatry, by which it had departed from God under King Jeroboam. Nor is it new for the Creator to use figurative language by translating names from a comparison of crimes. He also calls the rulers of Sodom the rulers of Judah and the people themselves the people of Gomorrah; and elsewhere: your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite, because of similar impiety, though he had once called them his own sons: I have begotten and exalted sons. So Egypt is sometimes understood as the whole world, in the record of superstition and curse. And Babylon in our John is a figure of the Roman city — great, proud in its kingdom, and a persecutor of God's saints. Therefore the magi are also titled by the name Samaritans, despoiled of what they shared with the Samaritans, as we said, idolatry. But against the king of the Assyrians, understand Herod, whom the magi certainly opposed at that time by not renouncing Christ, whom he was seeking to intercept.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the figurative nature of the prophecy. Pass A preserves the Latin syntax and nuances (e.g., 'the virtue of Damascus' for 'uirtutem Damasci'). Pass B provides appropriate scripture citations for the quoted/alluded passages (Isaiah 7:14, Zechariah 14:14, Psalm 72:15, Matthew 2:11) which were not explicitly numbered in the Latin but are clearly identifiable from the text. All clauses, including the discussion on the magi and the typology of Samaria/idolatry, are present.
